newsitem.title: USA: FDA studies unusual knee cartilage repair.
newsitem.headline: FDA studies unusual knee cartilage repair.

text.p: An innovative method of repairing cartilage, using the patient's own treated cells, helps people with knee injuries but more work is needed to understand why, a Food and Drug Administration advisory panel said on Thursday.

The FDA panel evaluating Genzyme's Carticel was faced with an unusual situation, judging a treatment that has already been on the market and available to patients and their surgeons for two years. The FDA is just beginning to regulate these new therapies, known as biologics, that use treated or manipulated human cells or tissues.

The FDA panel said more research is needed but that the early clinical results suggested that the procedure works better on certain knee injuries than conventional treatments, which orthopedists generally agree do not work very well.

However the panel said there was not yet enough research to determine whether Genzyme's innovative cell cultures caused the improvement in patients, or whether it was the overall surgery and physical therapy.

Repairing damaged knee cartilage has been one of the great unsolved challenges of orthopedics, but in the Carticel studies about 70 percent of the patients improved. Longer-term studies must establish how long the benefits last.

The Carticel procedure involves removing cartilage cells from the patient, culturing them to grow more cartilage, and then returning the cells to the site of the injury in surgery. Physical therapy is also required.

Panellists called for more study, and Genzyme said it plans more research. The company has already set up a registry to track all U.S. patients, and plans larger trials, tentatively involving 300 patients in a more rigorous comparison of the Carticel technique versus other therapies.

Genzyme, one of the leading U.S. biotech firms, estimates that up to 200,000 to 300,000 patients in the United States and Europe will be candidates for the treatment each year. The company estimates that each treatment will generate sales of $10,000.
However analysts say that the market will depend on how much acceptance Carticel gains from surgeons.

David Stone, an analyst at Cowen Inc., in Boston said most of the surgeons who have been trained in the technique have not yet used it. "Some are very enthusiastic -- a small group have done most of the treatments. But others think this is not ready for prime time yet," he said.

According to Genzyme, as of the end of 1996, a total of 1,463 orthopedic surgeons had been trained to use Carticel, and 463 insurance plans had agreed to cover it. It said 363 patients had been treated.
Genzyme vice president Dr. Richard Moscicki, told the panel the Carticel approach is "at least as good and probably better" than conventional treatments.
